title: Massive cuts to Via Rail come into effect leading to the rerouting of The Canadian and many intercity trains.
text: The Canadian is a transcontinental passenger train operated by Via Rail on its Western Canada service between Union Station in Toronto, Ontario, and Pacific Central Station in Vancouver, British Columbia, Canada. Canadian Pacific introduced this service on April 24, 1955, serving Montreal, Toronto and Vancouver.

title: The Tories introduce legislation that would create the Goods and Services Tax (GST), a national sales tax.
text: The goods and services tax is a value added tax introduced in Canada on January 1, 1991, by the government of Prime Minister Brian Mulroney. The GST, which is administered by Canada Revenue Agency (CRA), replaced a previous hidden 13.5% manufacturers' sales tax (MST).

title: Jean Charest resigns from cabinet after he was found to have spoken with a judge.
text: John James "Jean" Charest is a Canadian lawyer and former politician who served as the 29th premier of Quebec from 2003 to 2012. Prior to that, he was a member of Parliament (MP) between 1984 and 1998.

title: Ramon John Hnatyshyn replaces Jeanne Sauvé as governor general.
text: Jeanne Mathilde Sauvé was a Canadian politician, journalist and stateswoman who served as the 23rd governor general of Canada from 1984 to 1990 and as the 29th speaker of the House of Commons from 1980 to 1984. She was the first woman to hold either office, and is to date the only woman to serve as speaker of the House of Commons.

title: A controversial resolution is passed by the city council of Sault Ste. Marie, Ontario, declaring the city "English-only".
text: The Sault Ste. Marie language resolution was a government motion passed on January 29, 1990, by Sault Ste.

title: The federal government announces that it will privatize Petro-Canada; the legislation to do so is introduced in October..
text: Petro-Canada is a retail and wholesale marketing brand subsidiary of Suncor Energy. Until 1991, it was a federal Crown corporation.

title: A massive tire fire begins near Hagersville, Ontario. It takes 17 days to put out.
text: Tire fires are events that involve the combustion of large quantities of tires, usually waste tires, typically in locations where they are stored, dumped, or processed. They exist in two forms: fast-burning combustion and slow-burning pyrolysis that can continue for more than a decade.

title: 1990 Chambly by-election.
text: A by-election was held in the federal riding of Chambly in Quebec, Canada on February 12, 1990, following the resignation of Progressive Conservative Richard Grisé. Phil Edmonston won a huge victory pushing the PCs into third place becoming the first New Democratic Party Member of Parliament in Quebec.

title: Newfoundland Premier Clyde Wells confirms he will rescind Newfoundland's approval of the Meech Lake Accord.
text: The Meech Lake Accord was a series of proposed amendments to the Constitution of Canada negotiated in 1987 by Prime Minister Brian Mulroney and all 10 Canadian provincial premiers. It was intended to persuade the government of Quebec to symbolically endorse the 1982 constitutional amendments by providing for some decentralization of the Canadian federation.

title: The federal government decides that Sikhs may wear turbans while serving as Royal Canadian Mounted Police (RCMP) officers following the Baltej Singh Dhillon case.
text: Sikhs are followers of Sikhism, a religion that originated in the late 15th century in the Punjab region of the Indian subcontinent, based on the teachings of Guru Nanak. The term Sikh has its origin in the Sanskrit word śiṣya, meaning 'seeker', 'disciple' or 'student'.

title: Canadian arms designer Gerald Bull is assassinated in Brussels.
text: Gerald Vincent Bull was a Canadian engineer who developed long-range artillery. Bull moved from project to project in his quest to economically launch a satellite using a huge artillery piece, to which end he designed the Project Babylon "supergun" for Saddam Hussein's government in Iraq.

title: The World Wrestling Federation holds WrestleMania VI from SkyDome in Toronto, Ontario, drawing a crowd of 67,678.
text: Rogers Centre is a retractable roof stadium in downtown Toronto, Ontario, Canada, situated at the base of the CN Tower near the northern shore of Lake Ontario. Opened in 1989 on the former Railway Lands, it is home to the Toronto Blue Jays of Major League Baseball (MLB).

title: The Bloc Québécois Party is formed as several MPs led by Lucien Bouchard quit the Tories and Liberals.
text: Lucien Bouchard is a Canadian lawyer, diplomat and retired politician who was the 27th premier of Quebec from 1996 to 2001. Before his premiership in Quebec, he was a minister for two years in the Mulroney cabinet, Bouchard then founded and led the Bloc Québécois and became Leader of the Opposition in the House of Commons of Canada from 1993 to 1996.

title: The Edmonton Oilers win the 1990 Stanley Cup Final.
text: The Edmonton Oilers are a professional ice hockey team based in Edmonton. The Oilers compete in the National Hockey League as a member of the Pacific Division in the Western Conference.

title: Mikhail Gorbachev, President of the Soviet Union, arrives in Ottawa for a 29-hour visit.
text: Mikhail Sergeyevich Gorbachev was a Soviet and Russian politician who was the last leader of the Soviet Union from 1985 until the country's dissolution in 1991. He served as General Secretary of the Communist Party from 1985, and additionally as head of state from 1988.

title: Stanley Charles Waters is the first elected senator.
text: The Senate of Canada is the upper house of the Parliament of Canada. Together with the Crown and the House of Commons, they compose the bicameral legislature of Canada.

title: Elijah Harper prevents Manitoba from accepting the Meech Lake Accord.
text: Elijah Harper was a Canadian Oji-Cree politician who served as a member of the Legislative Assembly of Manitoba (MLA) from 1981 to 1992 and a member of Parliament (MP) from 1993 to 1997. Harper was elected chief of the Red Sucker Lake Indian Band in 1978, serving for four years and worked as a policy analyst prior to entering politics.

title: June 17–30 – Nelson Mandela tours North America, visiting three Canadian and eight U.S. cities.
text: Nelson Rolihlahla Mandela was a South African anti-apartheid revolutionary, politician, and philanthropist, who served as President of South Africa from 1994 to 1999. He was the country's first black head of state and the first elected in a fully representative democratic election.

title: Jean Chrétien elected leader of the Liberal Party of Canada at a leadership convention held in Calgary.
text: Joseph Jacques Jean Chrétien is a Canadian lawyer and former politician who served as the 20th prime minister of Canada from 1993 to 2003. He served as leader of the Liberal Party from 1990 to 2003 and as leader of the Official Opposition from 1990 to 1993.

title: Bob Rae's Ontario New Democratic Party wins a surprise majority in Ontario.
text: Robert Keith Rae is a Canadian politician and diplomat who served as the Canadian Ambassador to the United Nations from 2020 to 2025. Rae previously served as the 21st premier of Ontario from 1990 to 1995, leader of the Ontario New Democratic Party from 1982 to 1996, and interim leader of the Liberal Party of Canada from 2011 to 2013.

title: Roger Bacon becomes premier of Nova Scotia, replacing John Buchanan.
text: Roger Stuart Bacon was a Canadian politician who served as the 21st premier of Nova Scotia from 1990 to 1991.

title: Brian Mulroney temporarily increases the size of the Senate to ensure passage of the GST.
text: Martin Brian Mulroney was a Canadian lawyer, businessman, and politician who served as the 18th prime minister of Canada from 1984 to 1993. He led the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada and served as a member of Parliament (MP) from 1983 to 1993.

title: Bob Rae becomes premier of Ontario, replacing David Peterson.
text: David Robert Peterson is a Canadian lawyer and former politician who served as the 20th premier of Ontario from 1985 to 1990. He was the first Liberal officeholder in 42 years, ending the Tory dynasty.

title: Jean Chrétien is returned to the House of Commons after winning a by election for the New Brunswick riding of Beauséjour.
text: The House of Commons of Canada is the lower house of the Parliament of Canada. Together with the Crown and the Senate of Canada, it forms the bicameral legislature of Canada.

title: The Oshawa Generals win their fourth (and first since 1944) Memorial Cup by defeating the Kitchener Rangers 4 to 3 . The final game was played at Copps Coliseum in Hamilton, Ontario
text: The Memorial Cup is the national championship of the Canadian Hockey League (CHL), a consortium of three major junior ice hockey leagues operating in Canada and parts of the United States. It is a four-team round-robin tournament played among the champions of the Ontario Hockey League (OHL), Quebec Maritimes Junior Hockey League (QMJHL) and Western Hockey League (WHL), and a host team, which alternates on an annua…

title: The Edmonton Oilers win their fifth (and most recent) Stanley Cup by defeating the Boston Bruins 4 games to 1. Brandon, Manitoba's Bill Ranford is awarded the Conn Smythe Trophy
text: The Stanley Cup is the championship trophy awarded annually to the National Hockey League (NHL) playoff champion. It is the oldest existing trophy to be awarded to a professional sports franchise in North America, and the International Ice Hockey Federation (IIHF) considers it to be one of the "most important championships available to the sport".

title: The Saskatchewan Huskies win their first Vanier Cup by defeating the Saint Mary's Huskies 24 to 21 in the 26th Vanier Cup played at Skydome in Toronto
text: The Saskatchewan Huskies are the athletics teams representing the University of Saskatchewan in Saskatoon, Saskatchewan. The university began their athletics program in 1907 and has competed with others since 1911.

title: The Winnipeg Blue Bombers win their tenth Grey Cup by defeating the Edmonton Eskimos 50 to 11 in the 78th Grey Cup at BC Place Stadium in Vancouver. Scarborough, Toronto's Warren Hudson is awarded the game's Most Valuable Canadian
text: The Grey Cup is both the championship game of the Canadian Football League (CFL) and the trophy awarded to the victorious team playing in the namesake championship of professional Canadian football. The game is contested between the winners of the CFL's East and West divisional playoffs and is one of Canadian television's largest annual sporting events.

title: Doug Flutie returns to Canada to play with the BC Lions.
text: Douglas Richard Flutie is an American former football quarterback who played professionally for 21 seasons. Flutie played 12 seasons in the National Football League (NFL), eight seasons in the Canadian Football League (CFL), and one season in the United States Football League (USFL).

title: The National Gallery of Canada acquires Barnett Newman's Voice of Fire for $1.8 million, causing a storm of controversy.
text: The National Gallery of Canada, located in the capital city of Ottawa, Ontario, is Canada's national art museum. The museum's building takes up 46,621 square metres (501,820 sq ft), with 12,400 square metres (133,000 sq ft) of space used for exhibiting art.

title: Swann by Carol Shields published
text: Carol Ann Shields was a Canadian novelist and short story writer. Her 1993 novel The Stone Diaries, which won the U.S. Pulitzer Prize for Fiction as well as the Governor General's Award in Canada.

title: The Evening News by Arthur Hailey
text: Arthur Frederick Hailey, AE was a British-Canadian novelist whose plot-driven storylines were set against the backdrops of various industries. His books, which include such best sellers as Hotel (1965), Airport (1968), Wheels (1971), The Moneychangers (1975), and Overload (1979), have sold 170 million copies in 38 languages.

title: A Tenured Professor by John Kenneth Galbraith
text: John Kenneth Galbraith, also known as J. K. Galbraith or Ken Galbraith, was a Canadian-American economist, diplomat, public official, and intellectual. His books on economic topics were bestsellers from the 1950s through the 2000s.

title: TekWar by William Shatner
text: William Shatner is a Canadian actor. From 1966 to 1994, he starred as Captain James T. Kirk in the Star Trek franchise, from his debut as the captain of the starship Enterprise in the second pilot of the first Star Trek television series to his final appearance as Captain Kirk in the seventh Star Trek feature film, Star Trek Generations.

title: Magic Casement by Dave Duncan
text: David John Duncan was a Canadian fantasy and science fiction author.

title: Golden Fleece by Robert J. Sawyer
text: Robert James Sawyer is a Canadian and American writer of science fiction. He is the author of 25 published novels, and his short fiction has appeared in magazines and journals such as Analog Science Fiction and Fact, Amazing Stories, On Spec, and Nature, in addition to several anthologies.

title: Medicine River by Thomas King
text: Thomas King is an American-born Canadian writer and broadcast presenter who most often writes about First Nations. Though he previously said that he was of partial Cherokee descent, King accepted findings by genealogists in 2025 that he has no Indigenous ancestry.

title: The Magic Machine: A Handbook of Computer Sorcery by Alexander Dewdney
text: Alexander Keewatin Dewdney was a Canadian mathematician, computer scientist, author, filmmaker, and conspiracy theorist. Dewdney was the son of Canadian artist and author Selwyn Dewdney and art therapist Irene Dewdney, and brother of poet Christopher Dewdney.

title: Whylah Falls by George Elliott Clarke
text: George Elliott Clarke is a Canadian poet, playwright and literary critic who served as the Poet Laureate of Toronto from 2012 to 2015 and as the Canadian Parliamentary Poet Laureate in 2016–2017. Clarke's work addresses the experiences and history of the Black Canadian communities of Nova Scotia and New Brunswick, creating a cultural geography coined "Africadia".

title: The Wild Blue Yonder by Audrey Thomas
text: Audrey Grace Thomas is a Canadian novelist and short story writer who lives on Galiano Island, British Columbia. Her stories often have feminist themes and include exotic settings.

title: L'Oursiade by Antonine Maillet
text: Antonine Maillet was a Canadian novelist, playwright and scholar. She was a member of the Privy Council for Canada and the first non-European recipient of the Prix Goncourt, among other accolades.

title: See 1990 Governor General's Awards for a complete list of winners and finalists for those awards.
text: The 1990 Governor General's Awards for Literary Merit were prizes awarded to authors in 1990. Each winner of the prize received $10000 and a specially bound edition of their book.

title: Books in Canada First Novel Award: Sandra Birdsell, The Missing Child
text: The Amazon Canada First Novel Award, formerly the Amazon.ca First Novel Award and the Books in Canada First Novel Award, is a Canadian literary award, co-presented by Amazon.ca and The Walrus to the best first novel in English published the previous year by a citizen or resident of Canada. It has been awarded since 1976.

title: Geoffrey Bilson Award: Kit Pearson, The Sky Is Falling
text: The Geoffrey Bilson Award for Historical Fiction for Young People is a Canadian literary award that goes to the best work of historical fiction written for youth each year. The award is named after Geoffrey Bilson, a writer of historical fiction for youth and a history professor at the University of Saskatchewan who died suddenly in 1987.

title: Gerald Lampert Award: Steven Heighton, Stalin's Carnival
text: Steven Heighton was a Canadian fiction writer, poet, and singer-songwriter. He is the author of eighteen books, including three short story collections, four novels, and seven poetry collections.

title: Marian Engel Award: Carol Shields
text: The Writers' Trust Engel/Findley Award is a Canadian literary award, presented by the Writers' Trust of Canada to an established Canadian author to honour their body of work. Presented for the first time in 2008 under the name Notable Author Award, the award was created by merging the formerly separate Marian Engel Award and Timothy Findley Award, which were presented to female and male nominees respectively.

title: Pat Lowther Award: Patricia Young, The Mad and Beautiful Mothers
text: The Pat Lowther Memorial Award is an annual Canadian literary award presented by the League of Canadian Poets to the year's best book of poetry by a Canadian woman. The award was established in 1980 to honour poet Pat Lowther, who was murdered by her husband in 1975.

title: Stephen Leacock Award: W.O. Mitchell, According to Jake and the Kid
text: The Stephen Leacock Memorial Medal for Humour, also known as the Stephen Leacock Medal for Humour or just the Leacock Medal, is an annual Canadian literary award presented for the best book of humour written in English by a Canadian writer, published or self-published in the previous year. The silver medal, designed by sculptor Emanuel Hahn, is a tribute to well-known Canadian humorist Stephen Leacock and is accom…
wiki: Stephen Leacock Memorial Medal for Humour

title: Trillium Book Award: Alice Munro, Friend of My Youth
text: Alice Ann Munro was a Canadian short story writer who was awarded the Nobel Prize in Literature in 2013. Her work tends to move forward and backward in time, with integrated short story cycles.

title: “Another Day in Paradise” by Phil Collins
text: "Another Day in Paradise" is a song written and recorded by the English musician Phil Collins. Produced by Collins along with Hugh Padgham, it was released as the first single from his number-one album ...But Seriously.
listen: Another Day in Paradise Phil Collins

title: “Downtown Train” by Rod Stewart
text: "Downtown Train" is a song by American singer-songwriter Tom Waits released on his ninth studio album Rain Dogs in 1985. The promo video, which was directed by Jean-Baptiste Mondino and produced by Andrea Ambandos, was filmed in black and white and features a cameo appearance by boxer Jake LaMotta.

title: “Opposites Attract” by Paula Abdul and The Wild Pair
text: "Opposites Attract" is a song by American singer Paula Abdul from her debut album, Forever Your Girl. It was released on November 17, 1989, as the sixth and final single from the album through Virgin Records.
listen: Opposites Attract Paula Abdul and The Wild Pair

title: “Escapade” by Janet Jackson
text: "Escapade" is a song by American singer Janet Jackson from her fourth studio album, Janet Jackson's Rhythm Nation 1814. It was written and produced by Jackson and Jimmy Jam and Terry Lewis.

title: “I Wish It Would Rain Down” by Phil Collins
text: "I Wish It Would Rain Down" is a song by English musician Phil Collins from his fourth solo studio album, ...But Seriously. The song was a chart success in early 1990, peaking at No.
wiki: I Wish It Would Rain Down
listen: I Wish It Would Rain Down Phil Collins

title: “Nothing Compares 2 U” by Sinéad O'Connor
text: "Nothing Compares 2 U" is a 1985 song written by American musician Prince for his project, The Family, featured on its 1985 debut album. It was popularized when Irish singer and songwriter Sinéad O'Connor covered it for her 1990 studio album, I Do Not Want What I Haven't Got.

title: “All I Wanna Do Is Make Love to You” by Heart
text: "All I Wanna Do Is Make Love to You" is a song by American rock band Heart. It was composed by veteran songwriter and producer Robert John "Mutt" Lange and released as the lead single from the band's tenth studio album, Brigade, in March 1990.
wiki: All I Wanna Do Is Make Love to You
listen: All I Wanna Do Is Make Love to You Heart

title: “Vogue” by Madonna
text: "Vogue" is a song by American singer Madonna from her soundtrack album I'm Breathless. Written and produced by herself and Shep Pettibone, it was inspired by voguing, a dance popularized in New York City in the late 1980s.

title: “It Must Have Been Love” by Roxette
text: "It Must Have Been Love", originally "It Must Have Been Love", is a song written by Per Gessle and performed by the Swedish pop duo Roxette. The power ballad became the duo's third number one hit in the United States, and is one of their best selling releases, being certified gold or platinum in a number of countries.
listen: It Must Have Been Love Roxette

title: “Do You Remember?” by Phil Collins
text: "Do You Remember?" is a song by the English drummer and singer-songwriter Phil Collins. It was released in April 1990 as the fourth single from his fourth solo studio album, ...But Seriously.

title: “Step by Step” by New Kids on the Block
text: "Step by Step" is a song by American boyband New Kids on the Block, released on May 10, 1990, by Columbia Records as the first single from the album of the same name. It is the group's biggest-selling hit single.
wiki: Step by Step (New Kids on the Block song)
listen: Step by Step New Kids on the Block

title: “I'll Be Your Shelter” by Taylor Dayne
text: "I'll Be Your Shelter" is a song by American singer Taylor Dayne from her second studio album, Can't Fight Fate. Written by Diane Warren and produced by Ric Wake, the song was released in 1990 by Arista Records as the third single from Can't Fight Fate.
listen: I'll Be Your Shelter Taylor Dayne

title: “Across the River” by Bruce Hornsby and the Range
text: "Across the River" is a song by American musical group Bruce Hornsby and the Range. The song was co-written by Bruce Hornsby and his brother John and was the first single released from the band's studio album, A Night on the Town.
listen: Across the River Bruce Hornsby and the Range

title: “Vision of Love” by Mariah Carey
text: "Vision of Love" is the debut single by the American singer-songwriter Mariah Carey, released on May 15, 1990, for her first album Mariah Carey. It was written by Carey and Ben Margulies, and produced by Rhett Lawrence and Narada Michael Walden through Columbia Records.

title: “Release Me” by Wilson Phillips
text: "Release Me" is a song written and performed by American pop group Wilson Phillips, released as the second single from their debut album, Wilson Phillips. The song reached number one on the US Billboard Hot 100 in September 1990 and spent two weeks at number one.

title: “Blaze of Glory” by Jon Bon Jovi
text: "Blaze of Glory" is the debut solo single of American singer-songwriter Jon Bon Jovi. It was released in July 1990 by Mercury Records as the lead single from his first solo album, Blaze of Glory.
wiki: Blaze of Glory (Jon Bon Jovi song)
listen: Blaze of Glory Jon Bon Jovi

title: “Something Happened on the Way to Heaven” by Phil Collins
text: "Something Happened on the Way to Heaven" is a song by English musician Phil Collins, released in April 1990 by Atlantic, Virgin and WEA from his fourth studio album, ...But Seriously. The song peaked at No.
wiki: Something Happened on the Way to Heaven
listen: Something Happened on the Way to Heaven Phil Collins

title: “Praying for Time” by George Michael
text: "Praying for Time" is a song written, produced, and performed by English singer and songwriter George Michael, released on Epic Records in the United Kingdom and Columbia Records in the United States in 1990. It was the first single from his second studio album, Listen Without Prejudice Vol.

title: “Suicide Blonde” by INXS
text: "Suicide Blonde" is the lead single from Australian rock band INXS's seventh studio album, X. It was released on 22 August 1990 in the United States and on 3 September 1990 in Australia.

title: “More Than Words Can Say” by Alias
text: "More Than Words Can Say" More Than Words Can Say" for promotional purposes) is a song by Canadian rock band Alias. It was released in 1990 as the second single from their debut eponymous album.
listen: More Than Words Can Say Alias

title: “Impulsive” by Wilson Phillips
text: "Impulsive" is a song by American vocal group Wilson Phillips. It was released in October 1990 via SBK Records as the third single from their eponymous debut studio album.

title: “Hold On” by Wilson Phillips
text: "Hold On" is a song by American vocal group Wilson Phillips, released on February 27, 1990, by SBK Records as the lead single from their debut studio album, Wilson Phillips. The song was written by Carnie Wilson, Chynna Phillips, and Glen Ballard and produced by Ballard.

title: “Poison” by Bell Biv DeVoe
text: "Poison" is the debut single of American vocal group Bell Biv DeVoe, released as the first single from their debut album of the same name. The song, in the style of new jack swing, a late-1980s/early-1990s hybrid of R&B, hip hop and swing, was the group's most successful.

title: “Cradle of Love” by Billy Idol
text: "Cradle of Love" is a song by the English rock singer Billy Idol, released in 1990 as the first single from his fourth studio album, Charmed Life. The song was written by David Werner and Idol, and was produced by Keith Forsey.

title: “Do Me!” by Bell Biv DeVoe
text: "Do Me!" is a song by American musical group Bell Biv DeVoe. The song was released in 1990 as the second single from the group's debut album, Poison.

title: “How Am I Supposed to Live Without You” by Michael Bolton
text: "How Am I Supposed to Live Without You" is a song co-written in 1982 by Doug James and Michael Bolton. The track was originally recorded by Laura Branigan in 1983, charting at number one in both the US and Canadian Adult Contemporary charts.
wiki: How Am I Supposed to Live Without You
listen: How Am I Supposed to Live Without You Michael Bolton

title: “Pump Up the Jam” by Technotronic
text: "Pump Up the Jam" is the opening track on the Belgian act Technotronic's first album, Pump Up the Jam: The Album. It was released as a single on 18 August 1989 by Swanyard and SBK Records and was a worldwide hit, reaching number 2 in the United Kingdom in late 1989 and on the US Billboard Hot 100 in early 1990.

title: “Close to You” by Maxi Priest
text: "Close to You" is a song by English reggae singer Maxi Priest, released in 1990 by 10 Records as the lead single from his fifth album, Bonafide. It was written by Priest with Gary Benson and Winston Sela, and produced by Handel Tucker, Geoffrey Chung and Lowell "Sly" Dunbar.

title: “Black Velvet” by Alannah Myles
text: "Black Velvet" is a song written by Canadian songwriters Christopher Ward and David Tyson and recorded by Canadian singer-songwriter Alannah Myles. It was released in July 1989 as the second single from Myles' first studio album, Alannah Myles, by Atlantic Records.

title: “Don't Know Much” by Linda Ronstadt featuring Aaron Neville
text: "Don't Know Much" is a song written by Barry Mann, Cynthia Weil and Tom Snow. Mann was the first to record the song in 1980, gaining a minor chart hit in the US. The song was made famous when it was covered as a duet by Linda Ronstadt and Aaron Neville in 1989.
listen: Don't Know Much Linda Ronstadt featuring Aaron Neville

title: “All Around the World” by Lisa Stansfield
text: "All Around the World" is a song by English singer, songwriter and actress Lisa Stansfield from her debut studio album, Affection. It was released as the album's second single in 1989 by Arista Records.
wiki: All Around the World (Lisa Stansfield song)
listen: All Around the World Lisa Stansfield

title: Road to Avonlea
text: Road to Avonlea is a Canadian television series first broadcast in Canada between January 7, 1990, and March 31, 1996, as part of the CBC Family Hour anthology series, and in the United States starting on March 5, 1990. It was created by Kevin Sullivan and produced by Sullivan Films in association with the CBC and the Disney Channel, with additional funding from Telefilm Canada.

title: Material World
text: Material World is a Canadian television sitcom, which aired on CBC Television from 1990 to 1993. In its first season, the show was a conventional sitcom, shot on videotape with a laugh track, but in subsequent seasons the show adopted a single-cam comedy drama format.

title: The Little Flying Bears
text: The Little Flying Bears is an animated television series produced by CinéGroupe and Zagreb Film. It was a Canadian production which originally aired in 1990.

title: Neon Rider
text: Neon Rider is a Canadian drama television series which aired between 1990 and 1995. Created by Winston Rekert and Danny Virtue, the show was about the title character, a psychologist named Michael Terry who, after writing a successful book on adolescent psychology, purchases his childhood friend's family ranch just outside of Mission, British Columbia to open a therapeutic residential treatment program for trouble…

title: Mom P.I.
text: Mom P.I. is a 1990–92 Canadian television comedy-drama series starring Rosemary Dunsmore, Stuart Margolin, Emily Perkins, and Shane Meier. Dunsmore plays eternal optimist Sally Sullivan, a recently widowed mother of two supporting her family as a waitress in a working-class diner, who talks her way into a job as assistant to grumpy, cynical private eye Bernie Fox.

title: Saying Goodbye
text: Saying Goodbye is a Canadian television drama anthology series, which aired on TVOntario in 1990. The series consisted of five half-hour short drama films about people grappling with death, either dealing with grief after the death of a loved one or confronting their own mortality.

title: E.N.G.
text: E.N.G. is a Canadian television drama, following the staff of a fictional Toronto television news station. The show aired on CTV from 1989 to 1994.

title: Are You Afraid of the Dark?
text: Are You Afraid of the Dark? is a children's horror anthology television series created by D. J. MacHale and Ned Kandel.
wiki: Are You Afraid of the Dark?

title: Max Glick
text: Max Glick is a Canadian television comedy-drama series, which aired on CBC Television from 1990 to 1991. Based on the Morley Torgov novel The Outside Chance of Maximilian Glick and its 1988 film adaptation, the series centred on Maximilian Glick, a young Jewish boy coming-of-age in Beausejour, Manitoba in the 1960s.

title: Fireman Sam
text: Fireman Sam is an animated children's television series about a fireman named Sam Jones, his fellow firefighters, and other residents of the fictional Welsh village of Pontypandy (a portmanteau of two real towns, Pontypridd and Tonypandy). It was broadcast for the first time in November 1987 on Welsh TV channel S4C and is shown in more than 155 countries across the world.

title: The Raggy Dolls
text: The Raggy Dolls is a British cartoon series which originally aired on ITV that aired from 1986 to 1994. The series is set in Mr Grimes' Toy Factory, where imperfect dolls are thrown into a reject bin.

title: Pope John Paul II begins an eight-day tour of Cape Verde, Guinea-Bissau, Mali, Burkina Faso and Chad.
text: Pope John Paul II was the head of the Catholic Church and sovereign of Vatican City from 16 October 1978 until his death in 2005. He was the first non-Italian pope since Adrian VI in the 16th century, as well as the third longest-serving pope in history, after St.

title: January 25–26 – The Burns' Day Storm kills 97 in northwestern Europe.
text: The Burns' Day Storm was an extremely violent windstorm that took place on Thursday–Friday 25–26 January 1990 over North-Western Europe. It is one of the strongest European windstorms on record and caused many fatalities, approximately one hundred deaths, with almost half of these on the British Isles alone.

title: Japan launches the Hiten spacecraft, the first lunar probe launched by a country other than the Soviet Union or the United States.
text: The Hiten spacecraft, given the English name Celestial Maiden and known before launch as MUSES-A (Mu Space Engineering Spacecraft A), part of the MUSES Program, was built by the Institute of Space and Astronautical Science of Japan and launched on January 24, 1990. It was Japan's first lunar probe, the first robotic lunar probe since the Soviet Union's Luna 24 in 1976, and the first lunar probe launched by a count…

title: The Pale Blue Dot photograph of Earth is sent back from the Voyager 1 probe after completing its primary mission, from around 3.5 billion miles away.
text: Pale Blue Dot is a photograph of Earth taken on February 14, 1990, by the Voyager 1 space probe from an unprecedented distance of over 6 billion kilometers, as part of that day's Family Portrait series of images of the Solar System. In the photograph, Earth's apparent size is less than a pixel; the planet appears as a tiny dot against the vastness of space, among bands of sunlight reflected by the camera.

title: The Space Shuttle Discovery places the Hubble Space Telescope into orbit.
text: Space Shuttle Discovery is a retired American Space Shuttle orbiter. The spaceplane was one of the orbiters from NASA's Space Shuttle program and the third of five fully operational orbiters to be built.

title: Steven Balbus makes his first discovery leading to elucidation of magnetorotational instability.
text: Steven Andrew Balbus is an American astrophysicist who is the Savilian Professor of Astronomy Emeritus at the University of Oxford and a senior research fellow at New College, Oxford. In 2013, he shared the Shaw Prize for Astronomy with John F. Hawley.

title: Earth-grazing meteoroid of 13 October 1990: A 44 kilogram, 41.5 km/s meteoroid passes above Czechoslovakia and Poland at 97.9 km. It is the first time calculations of the orbit of such a body based on photographic records from two distant…
text: On 13 October 1990, meteoroid EN131090, with an estimated mass of 44 kg, entered the Earth's atmosphere above Czechoslovakia and Poland and, after a few seconds, returned to space. Observations of such events are quite rare; this was the second recorded using scientific astronomical instruments and the first recorded from two distant positions, which enabled the calculation of several of its orbital characteristics.

title: Stephen Blumberg is arrested for stealing more than 23,600 books in North America.
text: Stephen Carrie Blumberg is best known as a bibliomane who lived in Ottumwa, Iowa. After being arrested for stealing more than 23,600 books worth US$5.3 million in 1990 (equivalent to about $13M in 2025), he became known as the Book Bandit and was recognized as the most successful book thief in the history of the United States.

title: An adaptation of Anton Chekhov's play Three Sisters opens at the Gate Theatre in Dublin with locally born Sinéad, Sorcha and Niamh Cusack in the title rôles and their father Cyril Cusack as Dr. Chebutykin.
text: Anton Pavlovich Chekhov was a Russian playwright, short story writer, and physician. Widely considered one of the greatest writers of all time, his career as a playwright produced four classics, and his best short stories are held in high esteem by writers and critics.

title: Alicia Girón García is the first woman to become director of the Biblioteca Nacional de España.
text: The Biblioteca Nacional de España is the national library of Spain. It is the largest public library in the country, and one of the largest in the world.

title: J. K. Rowling has the idea for Harry Potter while on a train from Manchester to London: "I was staring out the window, and the idea for Harry just came. He appeared in my mind's eye, very fully formed. The basic idea was for a boy who…
text: Joanne Rowling, better known by her pen name J. K. Rowling, is a British author, philanthropist, producer, and screenwriter. She is best known for writing Harry Potter, a seven-volume series about a young wizard and the best-selling book series in history, with over 600 million copies sold.

title: Nicci Gerrard marries Sean French in the London Borough of Hackney, to make up a writing team known as Nicci French.
text: Nicci French is the pseudonym of English husband-and-wife team Nicci Gerrard and Sean French (born 28 May 1959), who write psychological thrillers together. The couple met in 1989 while working at the New Statesman and published their first co-written novel, The Memory Game, in 1997.

title: Uncertain date – Austrian writer Ernest Bornemann is awarded the first Magnus Hirschfeld Medal for sexual research.
text: Ernst Wilhelm Julius Bornemann, also known by his self-chosen anglicisation Ernest Borneman, was a German crime writer, filmmaker, anthropologist, ethnomusicologist, psychoanalyst, sexologist, communist agitator, jazz musician and critic. In 1988, Ernest Bornemann argued that pedophilic acts involving neither physical nor psychological violence did not necessarily have negative consequences for the child.

title: Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum theft: Twelve paintings, collectively worth from $100 to $300 million, are stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston, Massachusetts by two thieves posing as police officers. This is the…
text: In the early hours of March 18, 1990, 13 works of art were stolen from the Isabella Stewart Gardner Museum in Boston. Security guards admitted two men posing as policemen responding to a disturbance call, and the thieves bound the guards and looted the museum over the next hour.

title: Robert Mapplethorpe's "The Perfect Moment" show of nude and homosexual photographs opens at the Cincinnati Contemporary Art Centre, in spite of accusations of indecency by Citizens for Community Values.
text: Robert Michael Mapplethorpe was an American photographer and artist. Best known for his black-and-white photographs, his work encompassed celebrity portraits, self-portraits, erotic photographs, and still lifes of flowers.

title: East Side Gallery, 105 paintings by 129 artists from 20 countries, is painted on the east side of the Berlin Wall in Germany following its abandonment. It includes Dmitri Vrubel's My God, Help Me to Survive This Deadly Love and Birgit…
text: The East Side Gallery memorial in Berlin-Friedrichshain is a permanent open-air gallery on the longest surviving section of the Berlin Wall in Mühlenstraße between the Berlin Ostbahnhof and the Oberbaumbrücke along the Spree. It consists of a series of murals painted directly on a 1,316 m long remnant of the Berlin Wall, located near the centre of Berlin, on Mühlenstraße in Friedrichshain-Kreuzberg.

title: John Keane is commissioned by the British Imperial War Museum as an official war artist in the Gulf War.
text: A war artist is an artist either commissioned by a government or publication, or self-motivated, to document first-hand experience of war in any form of illustrative or depictive record. War artists explore the visual and sensory dimensions of war, often absent in written histories or other accounts of warfare.
